It's your perception of sleep that's making you feel tired all day

How we feel about a night's sleep can have a bigger impact on mood and grogginess than actual hours of rest. Here's how to change your mindset to feel more energised. By Helen Thomson

If you slipped under the covers at 2am, knowing your alarm was set for 6am, how do you think you would feel the next morning? You may be imagining a day of aching eyes and clouded thoughts, but it is perfectly possible to wake up feeling clear-headed and positive, then spend the day happily socialising, or even doing a spot of exercise.

For most of us, this sounds like a dream. We live in a world obsessed with how little sleep we get and how rubbish that makes us feel. Many of us chase solutions – wearing eye masks, using blue-light filters, eating sleep-boosting probiotics – all in the pursuit of that golden 8 hours of sleep.

But what if the secret to feeling restored has little to do with how much we have actually slept? A wave of new research is suggesting that, in many cases, the way we think about sleep matters more than the hours we get. Simply believing you are well-rested can be enough to create the positive mental and physical benefits of a peaceful slumber. The question then becomes, how do you trick yourself into thinking you have slept better than you have? The answer may be easier than you think.

The power of mindset

The idea that a simple shift in perspective can leave you feeling rested might sound absurd, but two decades of research have established that mindset has a powerful influence on our health and behaviour. Teaching children to embrace a growth mindset – the belief that their abilities can improve with learning – is now common practice in UK schools after studies showed that young people who viewed their mind as malleable, rather than fixed, coped better with failure and were more willing to take on new challenges.

Likewise, a person's “stress mindset” is closely linked to their physical and mental health: those who view stress as energising, rather than debilitating, show more adaptive physiological responses to stress and tend to perform better under pressure. Perhaps the most well-studied demonstration of mindset is its contribution to the placebo effect, with substantial evidence showing that merely believing that something will make you feel better can produce measurable physiological changes, even in the absence of an active drug.

Given this surfeit of evidence showing how mindset shapes our waking lives, researchers have now begun to explore whether similar effects apply to sleep. While chronic bad sleep is linked to poor health, it has also become apparent that even one or two bad nights' rest can make us unhappy and reduce our reaction times, impairing skills like driving. Yet we are surprisingly poor judges of how well we have slept. This even applies long term, and researchers have established that some people develop an “insomnia identity”: more than a third of those who consider themselves insomniacs are, in fact, getting decent sleep. This has led several researchers to ask whether our beliefs and expectations about sleep itself can shape how we feel.

Last year, Samir Akre at the University of California, Los Angeles, and his colleagues tracked 249 people with depression for 13 weeks, taking note of both their actual sleep time using smartwatches and their self-reported sleep behaviour. The mismatch between the two sets of data was striking: many people claimed they had slept terribly, saying it had taken them a long time to get to sleep and that they had woken many times in the night. But the objective data showed that simply wasn't true.

Notably, when participants performed cognitive tests, it was the self-reported sleep quality that predicted how well they did, rather than the objective sleep metrics. In other words, the belief that they had slept badly impaired their thinking the next day more than the sleep itself.

This is one of several new studies hinting that the way we think about sleep has powerful effects on our subsequent emotions and cognition. In an earlier, slightly mischievous experiment, performed in 2021, researchers allowed 16 adults to sleep for 8 hours on one day, followed by 5 hours the next. Upon waking, a secretly manipulated clock informed the participants how much they had slept. They then rated their subjective sleepiness and took part in a vigilance test that recorded their reaction times.

Those who believed they had slept 8 hours – but who had actually slept only 5 – performed significantly better on the test compared with those who had got 8 hours but thought they had been asleep for 5. Making a person believe they had slept more poorly than they did reduced their reaction times by around 20 milliseconds. This, the team says, is equivalent to the kind of deterioration in performance you would see when someone has four nights of 5 hours' sleep or two nights with only 3 hours of sleep.

The participants' brain activity told an even more intriguing story. Slow-wave activity in the brain, called delta power, correlates with what we know as “sleep drive” – the urge to sleep. Delta power is slowest upon waking and increases throughout the day, pushing you to get some shuteye at night. As expected, delta power increased more in the daytime following the 5-hour sleep compared with the 8-hour rest. However, when participants thought they had slept longer than they did, there was a relative reduction in delta power during the day. It appears that simply believing you slept well has a powerful neurological effect, shifting your sleep drive and making you feel more alert for longer.

This all suggests that changing how we think about the amount of sleep we get might help us respond better to a lack of Zs. But to fully utilise this power, we also need to consider how people judge whether they have had a good or bad night's sleep.

Nicole Tang at the University of Warwick, UK, spotted a gap in our knowledge in this department. “When you talk to people about sleep quality, everybody thinks they know exactly what they are talking about. It's something so familiar, and yet we often have different ideas and different definitions of it,” says Tang.

She noticed that, when assessing sleep, people would not only talk about the rest they had, but also about how they had felt the day before or the morning after. All too often, she says, sleep experts concentrate on the nighttime hours. “We realised we needed to stretch the timespan to look at what was happening either side of sleep, as well as what happened during the night.”

Tang and her colleagues asked 100 good and bad sleepers to compare multiple sleep scenarios – with each made up of various parameters chosen at random by a computer – and choose which reflected the best night's sleep.

A typical scenario might say something like: “I did a lot yesterday, I felt positive when I went to bed. I felt moderately sleepy. My mind was blank, but I felt very comfortable lying in bed. It took me no time to fall asleep. I woke a number of times, but only very briefly. I slept for about 5.5 hours and I didn't dream. On waking, I felt motivated to get out of bed. During the day, I felt drowsy and my head felt cloudy. My mood was bad, and I was sociable.”

It may sound a little nonsensical, but by analysing the responses given over multiple trials, the researchers could tease apart which factors were the most influential in forming our judgement of sleep quality.

What they discovered was surprising: our thoughts about the quality of our sleep aren't determined solely by what happens at night. The person's “level of physical activity, their mood, their social ability, whether or not they can think straight” all affected judgements of sleep quality, says Tang.

Which got Tang thinking: if what happens during the day influences perceptions of the previous night's sleep, then perhaps a person's feelings about their sleep changes as the day unfolds.

To test this idea, she concocted a follow-up study, where 119 adults were asked to rate the quality of their previous night's sleep every 2 hours between 8am and 10pm. They were also asked to provide information about their mood, their physical and social activity and any pain or discomfort. Finally, at the end of the day, participants took a test that asked them to remember what they had reported at the beginning of the day.

More than 90 per cent of the participants changed their rating of how well they thought they had slept at least once. This wasn't down to forgetfulness – all those who had altered their rating remembered what they had put at the start of the day. Far from being a static figure, people's rating fluctuated as the day unfolded. What improved people's perceptions of their sleep most strongly? Physical activity.

“When people were engaged in more positive physical activity, their sleep-quality rating tended to go up,” says Tang. That held true even when they had experienced an objectively bad night's sleep. Tang suggests that even when you have had little sleep, dragging yourself to the gym isn't such a bad idea – it might positively reshape your memory of sleep, leading to beneficial knock-on effects.

After sleeping poorly, people tend to cancel meetings, avoid exercise and think they shouldn't go out, she says. All these thoughts are safety behaviours that put a boundary on what you do, but the research indicates this might also stop you from positively revising the way you see your sleep.

A lot of people don't realise that we are remarkably adept at coping with short-term sleep loss. “It's a resilience we have forgotten about,” says Tang. “If your concept of sleep quality is not as rigid, if you know you can change it, then you can help yourself feel better.” Essentially, a few nights' bad sleep doesn't break us – unless we believe it does.

How to change your perception of sleep

Most of the research on sleep mindset looks at what happens when you miss one or two nights' sleep. But it could also be helpful for people with long-term sleep struggles. That could be very impactful, because we know that chronic sleep problems carry serious health consequences, including an increased risk of diabetes, cardiovascular disease and dementia.

While there are many reasons why people may have long-term troubles with sleep, one factor can be as simple as short-term sleep loss spiralling into insomnia. Beliefs about poor sleep can become self-fulfilling: when people think they have slept badly, it can make them worried about not sleeping enough and anxious about the following night's sleep, says Tang. This can put the brain into a high arousal state, meaning that they are more easily woken up throughout the night, with bad sleep continuing as a result.

Actively reshaping your perception of last night's sleep the next day – through exercise, say – could help to break this cycle. Another way to do this seems to be through mindfulness.

In a study led by Jason Ong at Nox Health in Alpharetta, Georgia, researchers used EEG to examine the overnight brain activity of people before and after they completed eight weekly mindfulness sessions alongside daily practice. Their sleep improved, yet their brain showed increased activity associated with wakefulness during the night.

Ong says the researchers think that the mindfulness practice – which is a type of meditation that trains your mind to pay more attention to the experiences both inside and outside your body without judgement – changed the participants' mindset at night. When they woke up, they were better able to control their emotional response and avoid anxious thoughts, preventing the damaging spirals that often fuel insomnia. “From that standpoint… it's changing how they perceive or relate to the state of being asleep [or awake],” he says.

One final way to create a more positive mindset around sleep is to re-examine how many hours you think you need in the first place. Eight hours is often said to be the gold standard, but that isn't true for everyone (see “How much sleep do you actually need?”, below). “Even healthy sleepers may internalise an ideal – often 8 hours – that doesn't match their personal physiological needs, creating a subtle but persistent expectation gap,” says Carlos De Las Cuevas at the University of La Laguna in Spain. “Helping people recalibrate expectations can reduce worry and improve sleep satisfaction, even without increasing total sleep time.”

Of course, none of this is a reason to abandon good sleep-hygiene practices like avoiding bright screens before bed, making sure you see light at the beginning of the day and eating well.

The ideal would be to get more sleep in the first place, but where that isn't possible, it should be reassuring to know that all is not lost. A simple change in mindset may give you that much-needed energy boost, resetting your brain for a day of clarity and positivity and a night of peaceful slumber – even after an uncomfortably early rise.

How much sleep do you actually need?

Sleep anxiety can be fuelled by the perceived need to get 8 hours of sleep a night. But although that is often heralded as the magic number, many people can cope well with less.

Research has shown that cultural expectations play a huge role in how people appreciate sleep. People in pre-industrial agricultural societies typically get between 5.7 and 7.1 hours of sleep per night, and report being totally satisfied with their sleep quality. For those in industrial societies, there is little evidence of harm when you consistently get more than 6 hours, while those who sleep 7 hours a night tend to live longer than those who sleep for more extended periods.

Sleep anxiety can be caused by the belief that you need to get 8 hours of sleep a night. But while that's often said to be the magic number, many people can do well with less.

Research has shown that cultural expectations have a big effect on how people feel about sleep. People in farming societies before industrialisation typically sleep between 5.7 and 7.1 hours a night and say they're happy with their sleep quality. For people in industrial societies, there's little evidence that it's harmful to regularly sleep more than 6 hours, while people who sleep 7 hours a night tend to live longer than those who sleep for longer periods.

To find out how much sleep you need, think about a time in the past year when you were consistently getting the most sleep – or in the past 10 years, if you're 30 or older – and use that average amount as a starting point, says Michael Goldstein, co-director of sleep medicine at Harvard Medical School. “Importantly, only consider the actual time asleep and not the time you were in bed,” he says.

How you frame your nightly slumber can, perhaps counterintuitively, exert a more profound influence on your daytime mood and perceived energy levels than the actual duration of rest itself. Imagine, for instance, retiring to bed at the late hour of 2 a.m., knowing full well that your alarm is poised to shatter the tranquility at 6 a.m. How would you anticipate feeling the following morning? The instinctive response might be to envision a day plagued by heavy eyelids and a mind shrouded in mental fog. However, it is entirely feasible to awaken with a sense of mental clarity and optimism, ready to navigate the day with social engagement and even physical activity.

For many, this scenario seems like a pipe dream. We inhabit a culture seemingly fixated on chronicling our sleep deprivation and bemoaning its detrimental effects. The pursuit of the elusive eight hours of sleep has spawned a cottage industry of solutions – from eye masks and blue-light filters to sleep-enhancing probiotics – all aimed at achieving that restorative ideal.

But what if the key to feeling truly rejuvenated lies not so much in the quantity of sleep obtained, but rather in the quality of our perception of that sleep? A burgeoning body of research is increasingly suggesting that, in numerous instances, our cognitive appraisal of sleep holds greater sway than the objective hours accumulated. The mere belief that one is well-rested can suffice to engender the positive mental and physiological benefits typically associated with a night of restful slumber. The operative question, then, becomes: how does one effectively engineer a cognitive shift to perceive sleep as more restorative than it objectively was? The answer, perhaps surprisingly, may be more readily attainable than one might initially assume.

The notion that a simple alteration in perspective can induce a feeling of restedness may seem preposterous at first glance. However, two decades of rigorous investigation have firmly established the significant impact of mindset on our health and behavior. The implementation of growth mindset principles – the conviction that one's abilities can be cultivated through dedication and hard work – is now commonplace in educational settings, following studies demonstrating that students who embrace a malleable view of their cognitive capabilities exhibit greater resilience in the face of setbacks and a heightened willingness to embrace novel challenges.

Similarly, an individual's "stress mindset" is inextricably linked to their overall well-being. Those who perceive stress as a catalyst for growth, rather than a debilitating force, demonstrate more adaptive physiological responses to pressure and tend to perform optimally under demanding circumstances. Perhaps the most compelling demonstration of the power of mindset is its pivotal role in the placebo effect, with substantial evidence indicating that the mere belief that a treatment will yield positive results can trigger measurable physiological changes, even in the absence of an active pharmacological agent.

Given the wealth of evidence illustrating the extent to which mindset shapes our waking experiences, researchers have now turned their attention to investigating whether analogous effects manifest in the realm of sleep. While chronic sleep deprivation is unequivocally linked to a host of adverse health outcomes, it has also become increasingly evident that even a single night or two of inadequate rest can negatively impact mood and diminish reaction times, thereby impairing crucial skills such as driving. Yet, our subjective assessment of sleep quality is often surprisingly inaccurate, beset by cognitive biases. This phenomenon extends to the long term, with researchers identifying the emergence of an "insomnia identity" in some individuals: a significant proportion of those who self-identify as insomniacs are, in reality, obtaining adequate sleep. This discrepancy has prompted researchers to explore whether our beliefs and expectations surrounding sleep can, in and of themselves, shape our subjective experience.

In a study conducted last year, Samir Akre and his colleagues at the University of California, Los Angeles, meticulously tracked 249 individuals diagnosed with depression over a 13-week period, meticulously recording both their objective sleep duration, utilizing wearable smartwatch technology, and their subjective, self-reported sleep behavior. The disparity between these two datasets was striking: many participants vehemently asserted that they had endured a night of profoundly disturbed sleep, citing prolonged sleep latency and frequent awakenings throughout the night. However, the objective data painted a markedly different picture, revealing that these claims were largely unsubstantiated.

Crucially, when participants engaged in cognitive performance assessments, it was their subjective perception of sleep quality, rather than the objective sleep metrics, that proved to be the most accurate predictor of their cognitive performance. In essence, the belief that they had slept poorly demonstrably impaired their cognitive function the following day to a greater extent than the actual sleep deprivation itself.

This study is one of several recent investigations that hint at the profound impact of our cognitive framework surrounding sleep on our subsequent emotional and cognitive states. In an earlier, somewhat mischievous experiment conducted in 2021, researchers allowed 16 adult participants to sleep for eight hours on one night, followed by a curtailed five-hour sleep period the following night. Upon awakening, a deliberately manipulated clock provided participants with false feedback regarding their sleep duration. Participants then rated their subjective sleepiness and completed a vigilance test designed to measure their reaction times.

Those participants who were led to believe they had slept for eight hours – despite having only slept for five – performed demonstrably better on the vigilance test compared to those who had actually obtained eight hours of sleep but were misled into believing they had only slept for five. Inducing the belief that one has slept more poorly than they actually did resulted in a reduction in reaction times of approximately 20 milliseconds. According to the research team, this magnitude of performance decrement is comparable to that observed following four consecutive nights of five hours of sleep or two consecutive nights of only three hours of sleep.

An analysis of the participants' brain activity revealed an even more intriguing narrative. Slow-wave activity in the brain, specifically delta power, is correlated with what is commonly referred to as "sleep drive" – the physiological impetus to sleep. Delta power is at its nadir upon awakening and gradually increases throughout the day, driving the individual to seek sleep at night. As anticipated, delta power exhibited a greater increase during the day following the five-hour sleep period compared to the eight-hour rest period. However, when participants were led to believe that they had slept longer than they actually had, a relative reduction in delta power was observed during the day. This suggests that simply believing that one has slept well exerts a powerful neurological effect, modulating sleep drive and promoting a sense of alertness that persists for a longer duration.

Collectively, these findings suggest that modifying our cognitive framework surrounding sleep duration may enable us to better cope with periods of sleep restriction. However, to fully harness this potential, we must also consider the factors that individuals employ to judge whether they have experienced a good or bad night's sleep.

Nicole Tang at the University of Warwick, UK, identified a significant gap in our understanding of this particular aspect. “When discussing sleep quality with individuals, the assumption is often made that everyone possesses a shared understanding of the concept. It is a concept that is seemingly familiar, yet we frequently hold divergent ideas and definitions of it,” notes Tang.

She observed that, in evaluating sleep, individuals not only referenced the amount of rest obtained but also their subjective feelings both on the preceding day and the subsequent morning. All too frequently, she argues, sleep experts focus exclusively on the nocturnal hours. “We came to the realization that it was necessary to broaden the temporal scope to encompass events occurring both before and after sleep, in addition to those occurring during the night.”

Tang and her colleagues tasked 100 participants, comprising both good and poor sleepers, with comparing multiple sleep scenarios – each characterized by a unique combination of parameters randomly generated by a computer – and selecting the scenario that best represented a night of restful sleep.

A representative scenario might read as follows: “I engaged in a significant amount of activity yesterday, and I felt positive as I prepared for bed. I experienced a moderate degree of sleepiness. My mind was relatively clear, and I felt comfortable while lying in bed. I fell asleep rapidly. I woke up a number of times, but only for brief periods. I slept for approximately 5.5 hours and did not dream. Upon waking, I felt motivated to rise from bed. During the day, I felt drowsy, and my head felt clouded. My mood was negative, and I was unsociable.”

While this may appear somewhat nonsensical, by analyzing the responses provided across numerous trials, the researchers were able to disentangle the factors that exert the greatest influence on our subjective evaluation of sleep quality.

Their findings were rather unexpected: our perceptions of sleep quality are not solely determined by events occurring during the night. An individual's “level of physical activity, their mood, their social engagement, and their cognitive clarity” all contribute to their overall assessment of sleep quality, according to Tang.

This observation prompted Tang to consider the possibility that an individual's subjective perception of their sleep may evolve as the day unfolds.

To investigate this hypothesis, she designed a follow-up study in which 119 adult participants were asked to rate the quality of their previous night's sleep every two hours between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m. Participants were also asked to provide information regarding their mood, their physical and social activity levels, and any experiences of pain or discomfort. Finally, at the end of the day, participants completed a test designed to assess their recall of their earlier responses.

Remarkably, over 90 percent of the participants altered their rating of their perceived sleep quality at least once throughout the day. This was not attributable to forgetfulness – all those who had modified their rating accurately recalled their initial assessment. Far from being a static judgment, people's subjective perception of their sleep fluctuated as the day progressed. What factor most strongly contributed to improvements in people's perceptions of their sleep? Physical activity.

“When individuals engaged in greater levels of positive physical activity, their sleep-quality rating tended to increase,” notes Tang. This held true even when they had objectively experienced a poor night's sleep. Tang suggests that even when sleep-deprived, forcing oneself to engage in physical exercise may not be such a detrimental strategy – it may positively reshape one's memory of sleep, thereby leading to beneficial cascading effects.

Following a night of poor sleep, individuals often tend to cancel social engagements, avoid exercise, and believe they should refrain from going out, she explains. These thoughts represent safety behaviors that impose limitations on one's activities. However, the research suggests that such behaviors may also prevent individuals from positively revising their perception of their sleep.

Many individuals fail to recognize our remarkable capacity to cope with short-term sleep loss. “It's a resilience we have forgotten about,” says Tang. “If your conceptualization of sleep quality is less rigid, if you are aware that you can modify it, then you can help yourself feel better.” In essence, a few nights of inadequate sleep do not inherently break us – unless we allow ourselves to believe that they do.

While much of the research on sleep mindset focuses on the impact of missing one or two nights of sleep, it could also prove beneficial for individuals grappling with long-term sleep disturbances. Such an application could be particularly impactful, given the well-established association between chronic sleep problems and serious health consequences, including an increased risk of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and dementia.

While the etiology of long-term sleep problems is multifaceted, one contributing factor can be as simple as short-term sleep deprivation escalating into chronic insomnia. Beliefs surrounding poor sleep can become self-fulfilling prophecies: when individuals believe they have slept poorly, it can induce anxiety about future sleep deprivation and apprehension about the following night's sleep, says Tang. This can place the brain in a state of heightened arousal, rendering individuals more susceptible to awakenings throughout the night, thereby perpetuating the cycle of poor sleep.

Actively reshaping one's perception of the previous night's sleep the following day – through physical exercise, for instance – could help to break this vicious cycle. Another potential avenue for achieving this involves the practice of mindfulness.

In a study led by Jason Ong at Nox Health in Alpharetta, Georgia, researchers utilized EEG technology to examine overnight brain activity in individuals both before and after their participation in eight weekly mindfulness sessions, coupled with daily practice. While their sleep improved, their brain activity paradoxically exhibited increased activity associated with wakefulness during the night.

Ong posits that the mindfulness practice – a form of meditation that cultivates attentiveness to both internal and external experiences without judgment – may have altered the participants' mindset at night. Upon awakening, they were better equipped to regulate their emotional responses and mitigate anxious thoughts, thereby preventing the detrimental spirals that often fuel insomnia. “From that standpoint… it's changing how they perceive or relate to the state of being asleep [or awake],” he says.

One final strategy for cultivating a more positive mindset surrounding sleep involves re-evaluating one's perceived sleep requirements in the first place. While eight hours is frequently touted as the gold standard, this is not universally applicable (see “How much sleep do you actually need?”, below). “Even healthy sleepers may internalize an ideal – often 8 hours – that doesn't match their personal physiological needs, creating a subtle but persistent expectation gap,” says Carlos De Las Cuevas at the University of La Laguna in Spain. “Helping people recalibrate expectations can reduce worry and improve sleep satisfaction, even without increasing total sleep time.”

Of course, none of this should be interpreted as a rationale for abandoning established sleep-hygiene practices, such as avoiding exposure to bright screens before bedtime, ensuring exposure to natural light at the start of the day, and adhering to a healthy dietary regimen.

The ideal scenario would undoubtedly involve obtaining sufficient sleep in the first place. However, when this is not feasible, it should be reassuring to know that all is not lost. A simple cognitive shift may provide that much-needed energy boost, resetting your brain for a day characterized by clarity and positivity, and a night of restful slumber – even following an uncomfortably early awakening.

Sleep anxiety can be further exacerbated by the perceived need to get 8 hours of sleep a night. But although that is often heralded as the magic number, many people can cope well with less.

Research has shown that cultural expectations play a huge role in how people appreciate sleep. People in pre-industrial agricultural societies typically get between 5.7 and 7.1 hours of sleep per night, and report being totally satisfied with their sleep quality. For those in industrial societies, there is little evidence of harm when you consistently get more than 6 hours, while those who sleep 7 hours a night tend to live longer than those who sleep for more extended periods.

To figure out your ideal number, you should identify a time within the past year when you consistently had the most sleep – or in the past 10 years, if you are aged 30 or older – and use that average duration as an initial target, says Michael Goldstein, co-director of sleep medicine at Harvard Medical School. “Importantly, only consider the actual time asleep and not the time you were in bed,” he says.

Aynan sizning uyqu haqdagi tushunchangiz sizni kechayu kunduz charchatmoqda

Bizning tunda qanday uxlab dam olganligimiz haqidagi o'ylarimiz, amaldagi dam olish soatlaridan ko'ra kayfiyat va holsizlikka (karaxtlikka) kattaroq ta'sir ko'rsatishi mumkin. O'zini yanada g'ayratli his qilish uchun dunyoqarashni qanday o'zgartirish haqida. (Muallif: Helen Tomson)

Agar siz ertalab soat 6 ga budilnik qo'yilganini bilgan holda kechasi soat 2 da ko'rpaga o'ransangiz (uhlashga yotsangiz), o'zingizni ertasiga qanday his qilasiz deb o'ylaysiz? Balki ko'zlaringiz og'rib, fikrlaringiz xiralashgan(tuman bo'lgan) bir kunni tasavvur qilayotgandirsiz, lekin butunlay tiniq ong va pozitiv his-tuyg'ular bilan uyg'onib, kuningizni mamnuniyat bilan suhbat qurish hislarida yoki hattoki biroz jismoniy mashqlar bilan o'tkazish umuman imkonsiz narsa emas.

Ko'pchiligimiz uchun bu bir orzudek tuyuladi. Biz qanchalik oz uxlashimiz va bu bizni qanchalik yomon his qilishimiz orqasidan quvadigan dunyoda yashayapmiz. Ko'pchiligimiz qanaqadir yechimlarni izlaymiz - masalan ko'z niqoblarini taqib o'tirish, ko'k chiroq filtrlaridan foydalanish, uyquni yaxshilaydigan probiyotik moddalarni iste'mol qilish — bularning barchasi o'sha oltin 8 soatlik uyquni izidan tushish yo'lidagi harakatdir.

Lekin dam olganlik hissini tuya olishning siri aslida qancha vaqt uxlaganimiz bilan deyarli bog'liq bo'lmasa-chi? Bir qator yangi tadqiqotlar shuni ko'rsatmoqdaki, ko'p hollarda bizning uyqu haqidagi dunyoqarashimiz yoki fikrlarimiz biz uxlagan soatlardan ko'ra ko'proq ahamiyatga ega. Shunchaki o'zingizni yaxshi dam olganingizga ishontirish - tinch uyqu(mudrash)ning ijobiy ruhiy va jismoniy foydalarini yaratish uchun yetarli bo'lishi mumkin. Keyin esa savol tug'iladi: qanday qilib siz o'zingizni uxlaganingizdan ko'ra yaxshiroq uhlaganingizga ishontira olasiz? Bu savolning javobi siz o'ylagandan ko'ra osonroq.

Dunyoqarashning (fikrlash doirasining) kuchi

Nuqtai nazardagi oddiygina o'zgarish o'zingizni ruhan tetik (dam olgandek) his qilishingizga olib keladi degan tushuncha ehtimol bema'ni(mantiqsiz) bo'lib tuyular, biroq, yigirma yil davomidagi o'tkazilgan tadqiqotlar natijasida aniqlanishicha: idrok, ya'ni ruhiy holat, insoning sog'ligi hamda uning hulqiga juda kuchli ta'sir qila olar ekan. Buyuk Britaniya maktablarida o'z fikrlash doiralrini butkul qotib qolganlikdan ko'ra moslashuvchan tarzda idrok etadigan insonlar (bolalar) turli qiyinchilik va omadsizliklarni oson yengib o'tishi anglanganidan shom o'quvchilari orasida aqliy o'sish dunyoqarashini - va ularning imkoniyatlari o'rganish orqali rivojlanishi mumkinligiga ishonchini – shakllantirish hozirgi kunda keng tarqalgan.

Huddi shunday, shaxsning "stress holatini qa'bul qilishi" ularning jismoniy va ruhiy salomatligiga bevosita bog'liq: stressni holdan toydiruvchi(zaiflashtiruvchi) emes, balki energiya beruvchi hislat deb biladigan kishilar shunga eng yaxshi moslashuvchi fiziologik javoblarni namoyon qiladi shuning bilan birga deyarli bosim ostida ham o'z vazafasini eng zo'r tarzda bajaradi Balki bunday idrok etish holatining eng sinalgan va yaqqol ko'rinishi bo'lmish platsebo effekti – xatto g'ayrioddiy giyohand moddalarni qabul qilmagan xolatni unikal bir nimani tasireda deya ishontirib bittada foydasi borligiga ishonishi sezilarsre fizioligk ozshlarga obkelishiga ko'plab aniq misollar borligidir.

Ongning idrok etishi biznig qay holatda bedor bo'lishimizga dalolat etadigan ortiqcha darajada ko'p bo'lgan isbotlarga qaraganda, tadqiqotchilar ana endi buning o'xshash bo'lgan effekti uyquga ham t'asir ko'rsata olish olmasligini uzoqlikdan o'rgana boshlashdi. Surunkali yomon uyqu sog'lig'ga zarar keltirishi ma'lum bo'lishi bilan, u yana ma'lumki xatto umuman uxlamay o'tirishning bir yoki ikkta kechasi bizni baxtsiz qila olish bilan birgalikda – ma'lum reaksiyani bajarish holatimizning qisqarishiga va xaydashga o'xshsh malakalarning zararlanishiga (yomonlashishiga) obkeladi.

Biz shunga qaramang naqadar daxshatli tarzda uxlamasligimiz ustidan xukm eta olmaydiganlarmiz. Bu uzqa shunday davim etmoqda v tadqiqotlar isboplab berdiki bu uning “Uyqusizlik indentligi ” bo'lishkgi mumkun. Va hattoli uzlarining uyqusizliakka ko'chatiga uchrrashgni oylar bo'lishiga qrmay uchdan bir qusmnsi haqida oylidgala yaxshi holtla ham uxlamishayabd. Bu holatlar ba'zi bizninjg idrokimi bo'la oqamuz nima ixonishishmzga yoki bo'lsan uyqqu o'zini o'zi yarashishigan savol tushunshga.

O'tgan yili, Los-Anjelesdagi Kaliforniya universiteti xodimi Samir Akre va uning hamkasblari depressiyaga chalingan 249 kishini 13 hafta davomida kuzatib borishdi, ularning smart soatlar orqali haqiqiy uyqu vaqti hamda o'zlari xabar bergan uyqu holatini qayd qilib borishdi. Ikkala ma'lumotlar to'plami o'rtasidagi nomuvofiqlik (katta farq borligi) kishini hayratda qoldiradigan darajada edi: ko'p odamlar uxlay olishmaganligini, uxlashga ko'p vaqt ketganini va tunda ko'p marta uyg'onganligini da'vo qilishdi. Lekin ob'ektiv (haqiqiy) ma'lumotlar buning oddiygina noto'g'ri ekanligini ko'rsatdi.

Shuni ta'kidlash joizki, ishtirokchilar kognitiv testlarni (aqliy testlarni) topshirganlarida, ularning qanchalik yaxshi natija ko'rsatishini ob'ektiv uyqu o'lchovlari emas, balki ularning o'zlari xabar bergan "uyqu sifati" belgilab berdi. Boshqacha aytganda, yomon uxladik degan ishonch ertasi kuni ularning fikrlashiga haqiqiy uyquning yetishmasligidan ham ko'proq putur yetkazdi.

Bu o'ylaganingizdan ham osonroq bo'lishi mumkin.

Fikrlash kuchining ta'siri

Fikrlashingizni o'zgartirish o'zingizni tetik his qilishingizga olib kelishi g'alati tuyulishi mumkin. Ammo, tadqiqotlar shuni ko'rsatadiki, fikrlashimiz sog'ligimiz va xulq-atvorimizga katta ta'sir ko'rsatadi. Bolalarga o'sish fikrlashini o'rgatish – o'qish orqali yaxshilanish mumkinligiga ishonish – maktablarda keng tarqalgan. Tadqiqotlar shuni ko'rsatadiki, yaxshilanish mumkinligiga ishonadigan bolalar muvaffaqiyatsizlikka yaxshiroq bardosh berishadi va yangi narsalarni sinab ko'rishga ko'proq tayyor bo'lishadi.

Xuddi shunday, odamning "stress fikrlashi" ularning sog'lig'i bilan bog'liq. Stressni zararli emas, balki foydali deb biladigan odamlar stressga yaxshiroq bardosh berishadi va yaxshiroq natijalarga erishadilar. Platsebo effekti fikrlash qanday ishlashining yaxshi namunasidir. Biror narsa o'zingizni yaxshi his qilishingizga olib kelishiga ishonish, hatto u haqiqiy dori bo'lmasa ham, tanangizda haqiqiy o'zgarishlarga olib kelishi mumkin.

Fikrlash hayotimizga shunchalik ta'sir qilganligi sababli, tadqiqotchilar endi uning uyquga ham ta'sir qilishini o'rganishmoqda. Uzoq vaqt davomida etarli uxlamaslik sog'lig'ingiz uchun yomon. Ammo, hatto bir yoki ikki yomon tun ham bizni baxtsiz qilishi va reaksiyalarimizni sekinlashtirishi mumkin, bu esa haydash kabi narsalarga ta'sir qiladi. Biroq, biz qanchalik yaxshi uxlaganimizni bilishda unchalik yaxshi emasmiz. Ba'zi odamlar hatto aslida yaxshi uxlashsa ham, uyqusizlik bor deb o'ylashadi. Bu tadqiqotchilarni uyqu haqidagi e'tiqodlarimiz o'zimizni qanday his qilishimizga ta'sir qiladimi, degan savolni berishga undadi.

Albatta, bularning hech biri uyqudan oldin yorqin ekranlarga ta'sir qilishdan qochish, kun boshida tabiiy yorug'likka ta'sir qilishni ta'minlash va sog'lom ovqatlanish rejimiga rioya qilish kabi o'rnatilgan uyqu gigienasi amaliyotlaridan voz kechish uchun asos sifatida talqin qilinmasligi kerak.

Ideal stsenariy, shubhasiz, birinchi navbatda etarli uyqu olishni o'z ichiga oladi. Biroq, bu mumkin bo'lmaganda, hammasi yo'qolmaganligini bilish ishonchli bo'lishi kerak. Oddiy kognitiv o'zgarish sizga kerakli energiya kuchini berishi, miyangizni tiniqlik va ijobiylik bilan ajralib turadigan kun va dam olish kechasi uchun qayta tiklashi mumkin – hatto noqulay erta uyg'ongandan keyin ham.
